# The Mathematics of Portfolio Return (continued)

## MONEY-WEIGHTED RETURNS (MWRs) {#a}

Unfortunately, in the event of external cash flows we cannot continue to use the ratio of market values to calculate wealth ratios and hence rates of return. The cash flow itself will contribute to the valuation. Therefore, we must develop alternative methodologies that adjust for external cash flow.

> **Note**
>
> External cash flow represents capital (cash or assets) that enters or exits a portfolio. Internal cash flow includes dividends and coupon payments retained within the portfolio, corporate actions and normal transactions within the portfolio.

### Internal rate of return (IRR) {#b}

To allow for external cash flow we can borrow a methodology used throughout finance, the "internal rate of return" or IRR.

The internal rate of return has been used for many decades to assess the value of capital investment or other business ventures over the future lifetime of a project. John Maynard Keynes, (Keynes, *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money* (1936).) the famous economist, first suggested the use of IRR to justify an investment in the context of market comparison. (Magni, "Average Internal Rate of Return and Investment Decisions: A New Perspective" (2010).)

> **Note**
>
> It is perhaps less well known that Keynes was a hugely successful institutional investor, managing the Kings College Cambridge Endowment fund between 1921 and his death in 1946, achieving an annualised outperformance of 8% and influencing many investment management giants such as Warren Buffett, George Soros and David Swensen. (Chambers and Dimson, "John Maynard Keynes, Investment Innovator" (2013).)

Normally the initial outlay, estimated costs and expected gains of a project are well known and the internal rate of return can be calculated to determine whether the investment is worth undertaking. IRR is also used to calculate the future rate of return on a bond, which is called the yield to redemption.

### Ex-ante internal rate of return {#c}

The formal definition of the IRR is the discount rate that makes the net present value equal to zero in a discounted cash flow analysis. Used in this context, this return calculation methodology is best described as an ex-ante IRR, primarily used to aid imminent investment decisions. It's not difficult to understand why actuaries based at insurance companies and pension funds concerned about forecast actuarial return might turn to IRR to measure portfolio returns ex-post.

> **⚠ Caution**
>
> If you trawl through published financial literature on the internal rate of return it will undoubtedly reference the ex-ante IRR.

There are many criticisms of IRR as a method, including:

1. It is difficult to calculate, requiring an iterative approach
2. Its multiple potential solutions
3. Its constant rate of return assumption
4. Its assumption that future cash flows will be reinvested in the continuing rate of return
5. The opportunity for the return calculation to be manipulated

Today, spreadsheets offer easy solutions to IRR calculations. However, historically solutions were more difficult to obtain; there were no direct solutions and time-consuming iterative methods had to be employed. Controversy surrounds the authorship of early iterative methods, in particular the Newton—Raphson method (Named after the famous physicist Sir Isaac Newton. Newton may have been a great physicist and Master of the Royal Mint, but he was not such a great investor. In 1720, Newton, carried away with profits made by colleagues, invested much of his personal fortune in the South Sea Company. This company was responsible for perhaps the world's first financial crash, in the Autumn of 1720. Newton lost close to £40 million in today's money. Newton forbade anyone to ever utter the words "South Sea" in his presence and famously complained he "could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people".), which perhaps should be attributed to Thomas Simpson. (Kollerstrom, "Thomas Simpson and Newton's Method of Approximation: An Enduring Myth" (1992).) Of course, ultimately all iterative methods will achieve the same answer, just with more or less efficiency.

> **Note**
>
> Excel® offers two IRR functions, IRR and XIRR (extended IRR). The IRR function assumes regular periods; for most performance return calculations the XIRR function will be more appropriate.

> **Note**
>
> Performance analysts analyse historic, ex-post performance and are therefore less concerned about ex-ante IRR and more concerned about the calculation of ex-post IRR.

Multiple potential solutions are indeed possible, (Fischer and Wermers, *Performance Evaluation and Attribution of Security Portfolios* (2013), p. 340.) but you need to work very hard, with quite extreme data, to generate suitable examples. Potential solutions are technically possible for each change in sign of cash flow data over a period of analysis but are extremely unlikely to be experienced in practice.

The assumption of a constant force of return throughout the period of measurement is a real problem. We know markets are volatile, therefore we know this assumption is not true. For the ex-ante assessment of a future project or investment, a constant force of return assumption is appropriate, but for ex-post analysis of asset performance it is much more problematic. This assumption also means we cannot disaggregate the IRR into different asset categories since we cannot continue to use a single constant rate for each asset category. This is a major problem for attribution analysis.

The reinvesting of future cash flows in the continuing rate of return is a problem specifically for ex-ante IRR and not ex-post IRR. Ex-post analysis of a self-contained portfolio of assets or a single asset need not be concerned about how ex-post cash flows have been invested. Even the reinvestment assumption in ex-ante IRR can be challenged — see the work of Magni and Martin. (Magni and Martin, "The Reinvestment Assumption Fallacy for IRR and NPV: A Pedagogical Note" (December 2017).)

The manipulation of IRRs is a controversial area. Clearly delaying capital calls and returning capital to asset owners earlier will enhance the IRR (some might describe controlling the timing of cash flow in this manner good management, not manipulation). However, to the extent that the asset manager has control over the timing of cash flows, the opportunity to manipulate returns exists. Phalippou suggests:

> IRR is probably the worst performance metric one may use in an investment context. It exaggerates the variation across funds, exaggerates the performance of the best funds, can be readily inflated, and provide perverse incentives to fund managers. (Phalippou, "The Hazards of Using IRR to Measure Performance" (2008).)

### Simple internal rate of return {#d}

For a single period, the IRR method in its most simple form requires that a return $r$ be found that satisfies the following equation:

$$V_E = V_S \times (1 + r) + C \times (1 + r)^{0.5} \tag{3.13}$$

where $C$ = external cash flow.

In this form we are assuming that all cash flows are received at the mid-point of the period under analysis. To calculate the simple IRR, we need only the start and end market values and the total external cash flow, as shown in Exhibit 3.4.

### Exhibit 3.4 Simple IRR {#e}

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Market start value | $74.2m |
| Market end value | $104.4m |
| External cash flow | $37.1m |

$$104.4 = 74.2 \times (1 + r) + 37.1 \times (1 + r)^{0.5}$$

We can see that $r = -7.41\%$ satisfies the above equation.

$$74.2 \times (0.9259) + 37.1 \times (0.9259)^{0.5} = 104.4$$

### Ex-post internal rate of return {#f}

Assuming that all cash flows are received midway through the period of analysis is a fairly crude estimate. The mid-point assumption can be modified for all cash flows to adjust for the fraction of the period of measurement that the cash flow is available for investment as follows:

$$V_E = V_S \times (1 + r) + \sum_{t=1}^{t=T} C_t \times (1 + r)^{W_t} \tag{3.14}$$

where:

- $C_t$ = the external cash flow on day $t$
- $W_t$ = weighting ratio to be applied on day $t$

Obviously, there will be no external cash flow for most days:

$$W_t = \frac{TD - D_t}{TD} \tag{3.15}$$

where:

- $TD$ = total number of days within the period of measurement
- $D_t$ = number of days since the beginning of the period, including weekends and public holidays

In addition to the information in Exhibit 3.4 to calculate the ex-post internal rate of return shown in Exhibit 3.5, we need to know the date of the cash flow and the length of the period of analysis.

IRR is an example of a money-weighted return methodology; each amount or dollar invested is assumed to achieve the same effective rate of return irrespective of when it was invested.

### Exhibit 3.5 Ex-post IRR {#g}

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market start value | 31 December | $74.2m |
| Market end value | 31 January | $104.4m |
| External cash flow | 14 January | $37.1m |

Assuming the cash flow is at the end of day 14:

$$104.4 = 74.2 \times (1 + r) + 37.1 \times (1 + r)^{\frac{17}{31}}$$

We can see that $r = -7.27\%$ satisfies the above equation.

$$74.2 \times (0.9273) + 37.1 \times (0.9273)^{\frac{17}{31}} = 104.4$$

In the US the term "dollar-weighted" rather than "money-weighted" may be used; however, the term "money-weighted" is increasingly common in the US and is used worldwide.

> **Note**
>
> The weight of money invested at any point of time will ultimately impact the final return calculation. Therefore, if using this methodology, it is important to perform well when the amount of money invested is largest.

For the simple internal rate of return only, the solution of the quadratic equation can be used:

$$\text{Quadratic formula} \quad x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \tag{3.16}$$

where $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$

Let $x = (1 + r)^{0.5}$

Using data from Exhibit 3.4 in Exhibit 3.6:

### Exhibit 3.6 Simple IRR — using quadratic formula {#h}

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Market start value | $74.2m |
| Market end value | $104.4m |
| External cash flow | $37.1m |

$$74.2 \times (1 + r) + 37.1 \times (1 + r)^{0.5} - 104.4 = 0$$

$$(1 + r)^{0.5} = \frac{-37.1 \pm \sqrt{37.1^2 - 4 \times 74.2 \times -104.4}}{2 \times 74.2} = \frac{-37.1 + 179.895}{148.4} = 0.96223$$

Therefore $r = -7.41\%$, the same as in Exhibit 3.4.

### Simple Dietz {#i}

Even in its simple form the internal rate of return is not a particularly practical calculation, especially over longer periods with multiple cash flows. Peter Dietz (Dietz, *Pension Funds: Measuring Investment Performance* (1966).) suggested as an alternative the following simple adaptation of Equation 3.2 to adjust for external cash flow:

$$r = \frac{V_E - V_S - C}{V_S + C/2} \tag{3.17}$$

This is now known as the simple (or original) Dietz method.

The numerator of Equation 3.17 represents the investment gain (or loss) in the portfolio. In the denominator, replacing the initial market value we now use the average capital invested represented by the initial market value plus half the external cash flow. An assumption has been made that the external cash flow is invested midway through the period of analysis and has been weighted accordingly.

> **⚠ Caution**
>
> The average capital invested is absolutely not the average of the start and end values which would factor in an element of portfolio return into the denominator.

To calculate a simple Dietz return, like the simple IRR, only the start market value, end market value and total external cash flow are required, as shown in Exhibit 3.7.

### Exhibit 3.7 Simple Dietz {#j}

Using the existing example data:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Market start value | $74.2m |
| Market end value | $104.4m |
| External cash flow | $37.1m |

The simple Dietz rate of return is:

$$\frac{104.4 - 74.2 - 37.1}{74.2 + 37.1/2} = \frac{-6.9}{92.75} = -7.44\%$$

Dietz originally described his method as assuming that one half of the net contributions are made at the beginning of the time interval and one half at the end of the time interval:

$$r = \frac{V_E - C/2}{V_S + C/2} - 1 \tag{3.18}$$

This simplifies to the more common description:

$$r = \frac{V_E - C/2}{V_S + C/2} - \frac{V_S + C/2}{V_S + C/2} = \frac{V_E - V_S - C}{V_S + C/2} \tag{3.19}$$

The Dietz method is easier to calculate and easier to visualise than the IRR method, and it can also be disaggregated, that is to say, the total return is the sum of the individual parts.

### ICAA method {#k}

The Investment Counsel Association of America (ICAA) proposed a straightforward extension of the simple Dietz method (Investment Counsel Association of America, "The Standards of Measurement and Use for Investment Performance Data" (1971).) as follows:

$$r = \frac{V_E' - V_S - C' + I}{V_S + \frac{C'}{2}} \tag{3.20}$$

where:

- $I$ = total portfolio income
- $C'$ = external cash flow including any reinvested income
- $V_E'$ = market end value including any reinvested income

The standard example is extended to the ICAA method in Exhibit 3.8.

### Exhibit 3.8 ICAA method {#l}

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Market start value | $74.2m |
| Market end value | $104.2m |
| External cash flow | $37.1m |
| Total income | $0.4m |
| Income reinvested | $0.2m |

$$\frac{104.2 - 74.2 - (37.1 + 0.2) + 0.4}{74.2 + (37.1+0.2)/2} = \frac{-6.9}{92.85} = -7.43\%$$

In this method, income (equity dividends, interest or coupon payments) is not automatically assumed to be available for reinvestment. The gain in the numerator is appropriately adjusted for any reinvested income included in the final value by including reinvested income in the definition of external cash flow.

Interestingly, although the average capital is increased for any reinvested income in the denominator there is no negative adjustment for any income not reinvested. This is perhaps not unreasonable from the perspective of the client if the income is retained and not paid until the end of period.

However, from the asset manager's viewpoint, if this income is not available for reinvestment it should be treated as a negative cash flow as follows:

$$r = \frac{V_E - V_S - C + I}{V_S + \frac{(C - I)}{2}} \tag{3.21}$$

Extending our previous example again in Exhibit 3.9:

### Exhibit 3.9 Income unavailable {#m}

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Market start value | $74.2m |
| Market end value | $104.0m |
| External cash flow | $37.1m |
| Total income | $0.4m |

$$\frac{104.0 - 74.2 - 37.1 + 0.4}{74.2 + (37.1-0.4)/2} = \frac{-6.9}{92.55} = -7.46\%$$

In Equation 3.21 any income received by the portfolio is assumed to be unavailable for investment by the asset manager and transferred to a separate income account for later payment or alternatively paid directly to the client.

Obviously, income paid or transferred is no longer included in the final value, $V_E$, of the portfolio. In effect, in this methodology income is treated as negative cash flow. Since income is normally always positive, this method has the effect of reducing the average capital employed, decreasing the size of the denominator, and thus leveraging (or gearing) the final rate of return. Consequently, this method should only be used if portfolio income is genuinely unavailable to the asset manager for further investment. Typically, this method is used to calculate the return of an asset category (sector or component) within a portfolio.

### Modified Dietz {#n}

Assuming that all cash flows are received midway through the period of analysis is a fairly crude estimate. The simple Dietz method can be further modified by day-weighting each cash flow by the following formula to establish a more accurate average capital employed.

$$r = \frac{V_E - V_S - C}{V_S + \sum C_t \times W_t} \tag{3.22}$$

where:

- $C$ = total external cash flow within period
- $C_t$ = external cash flow on day $t$
- $W_t$ = weighting ratio to be applied to external cash flow on day $t$

$$W_t = \frac{TD - D_t}{TD} \quad \text{(Equation 3.15, from earlier)}$$

where:

- $TD$ = total number of days within the period of measurement
- $D_t$ = number of days since the beginning of the period, including weekends and public holidays

In determining $D_t$ the performance analyst must establish if the cash flow is received at the beginning or end of the day. If the cash flow is received at the start of the day, then it is reasonable to assume that the portfolio manager is aware of the cash flow and is able to respond to it; therefore it is reasonable to include this day in the weighting calculation. On the other hand, if the cash flow is received at the end of the day the portfolio manager is unable to take any action at that point and therefore it is unreasonable to include the current day in the weighting calculation.

For example, take a cash flow received on the 14th day of a 31-day month. If the cash flow is at the start of the day, then there are 18 full days including the 14th day available for investment and the weighting factor for this cash flow should be $(31 - 13)/31$. Alternatively, if the cash flow is at the end of the day, then there are 17 full days remaining and the weighting factors should be $(31 - 14)/31$. Day counts include weekends and public holidays.

Performance analysts should determine a company policy and apply this consistently to all cash flows.

Fisher and Wermers (Fischer and Wermers, "Performance Evaluation and Attribution of Security Portfolios" (2013).) demonstrate that the modified Dietz method is, in fact, a first-order linear approximation to the IRR. A second-order approximation is available, but is more complex to calculate, less practical to use, and the modified Dietz method is already a good approximation. The Dietz methods are therefore both money-weighted methodologies.

> **⚠ Caution**
>
> The modified Dietz method is sometimes erroneously described as an approximation of the time-weighted rate of return. The modified Dietz method is a money-weighted rate of return and can be accurately described as an approximation of the internal rate of return.

The modified Dietz return is calculated using our standard example data in Exhibit 3.10.

### Exhibit 3.10 Modified Dietz {#o}

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market start value | 31 December | $74.2m |
| Market end value | 31 January | $104.4m |
| External cash flow | 14 January | $37.1m |

Assuming the cash flow is at the end of day 14:

$$\frac{104.4 - 74.2 - 37.1}{74.2 + \frac{(31 - 14)}{31} \times 37.1} = \frac{-6.9}{94.55} = -7.30\%$$

Assuming the cash flow is at the beginning of day 14 with 18 full days in the month left:

$$\frac{104.4 - 74.2 - 37.1}{74.2 + \frac{(31 - 13)}{31} \times 37.1} = \frac{-6.9}{95.74} = -7.21\%$$
